subject: Sanskrit
text: Shuchiparyavaranam (Pure Environment) describes environmental pollution and its causes. Factories emit smoke (dhoom), garbage (kachra), and plastic pollute air, water, and earth. Rivers are filled with filth. Forests are being cut. Birds and animals are disappearing. Key verse: 'Prastartal baddhang nagaram idam praanashunyamiva' meaning the city bound in stone layers appears lifeless. Conservation duty: everyone must plant trees (vriksha ropan), save water (jal sanrakshan), and respect nature. Clean environment is the foundation of healthy life. Important vocabulary: paryavaranam = environment, shuchi = clean, vriksha = tree, nadi = river, pradushan = pollution, sanrakshan = conservation.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Buddhirbalavati Sada means intelligence is always more powerful than physical strength. Story: a mother and her son get trapped in a forest. A lion approaches. The intelligent mother tells the lion to eat her five other sons first and she will come back for herself. The lion agrees and they escape. Key shloka: 'Buddhiryasya balam tasya nirbuddhesha kuto balam' meaning one who has intelligence has strength; where is strength for the one without intelligence? The story teaches that quick thinking and wisdom overcome physical danger. Bravery alone is insufficient; combined with intelligence it becomes invincible.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Vyayamah Sarvada Pathyah means exercise is always beneficial. Regular exercise (vyayam) keeps the body healthy, strong, and disease-free. One who exercises regularly does not feel fatigue easily and can do more work. Exercise removes laziness (aalasya) and sharpens the intellect (buddhi). Sushrutacharya said: 'Sarveshameva shokanam upayo vyayam eva hi' meaning exercise is the remedy for all troubles. Best time for exercise: at sunrise (suryodaya). Excessive exercise is also harmful - moderate amount (madhyam matra) is ideal. Important vocabulary: vyayam = exercise, balam = strength, swasthya = health, rogamukt = disease-free, surya = sun.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Shishulalanam (Nurturing of a Child) describes the beautiful bond between mother and infant. The mother loves and nurtures her child, feeds it milk, and delights in its babbling speech (tutlati boli). The child smiling is the mother greatest joy. The child is compared to a lotus flower (kamal), the moon (chandra), and a celestial deity (devata). Mother love is infinite and incomparable. Key themes: maternal love, innocence of childhood, the sacred mother-child bond. Important vocabulary: shishu = infant, mata = mother, sneha = affection, dugdh = milk, hasya = smile, lalanam = nurturing.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Janani Tulyavatsala means a mother loves all her children equally. This lesson is based on a Mahabharata episode. Kunti has five Pandava sons and loves them all equally. When Arjuna faces danger, she grieves deeply showing that no child is greater or lesser in a mother eyes. Key shloka: 'Putranam janani tulyameva vatsala bhavet' meaning a mother has equal affection for all her sons. Message: all family members should be treated equally with equal care and affection. Discrimination among children is against the natural law of motherhood. Important vocabulary: janani = mother, putra = son, vatsalya = maternal love, samata = equality, sneha = affection.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Subhashitani means good sayings or wise maxims. Key shlokas and their meanings: (1) 'Vidya dadati vinayam, vinayad yati patratam' - Education gives humility; from humility comes worthiness. (2) 'Satyam bruyat priyam bruyat na bruyat satyamApriyam' - Speak truth, speak pleasantly, do not speak unpleasant truth harshly. (3) 'Alasasya kuto vidya, avidyasya kuto dhanam' - Where is knowledge for the lazy? Where is wealth for the uneducated? (4) 'Ahimsa paramo dharmah' - Non-violence is the highest duty. (5) 'Vasudhaiva kutumbakam' - The whole world is one family. (6) 'Utsahe hi vasate lakshmi' - Goddess Lakshmi (prosperity) resides in enthusiasm. These maxims are timeless guides for right living.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Sauhardang Prakriteh Shobha (Harmony is the Beauty of Nature) is a one-act play showing friendship and cooperation between animals in a forest. Characters: Singh (lion), Harit (deer), Kak (crow), Mushak (mouse). When one animal faces danger the others help. Key message: all creatures in nature are interdependent. Cooperation and love (maitri) make life beautiful. Conflict and enmity destroy life. Key shloka: 'Sauhardameva jagatah shobha' - The beauty of the world is good-will alone. Themes: friendship (maitri), mutual help (sahayog), non-violence, interdependence of all living beings.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Vichitrah Sakshi (The Strange Witness) is a justice story. A merchant deposits money with someone. When he asks for it back the person denies receiving it. The case goes before a judge. The merchant cleverly names a tree as witness saying the money was given sitting under that tree. The defendant goes to the tree and takes time to return. The judge understands that the defendant went to retrieve the hidden money from there. He is proved guilty. Justice wins through intelligence. Themes: truth always wins (satya ki vijay), judicial wisdom, cleverness and quick thinking. Vocabulary: sakshi = witness, nyay = justice, dhan = money, vruksha = tree, apakarmi = wrongdoer.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Sandhi (junction) is the combination of two sounds/syllables resulting in modification. Three main types: (1) Svar Sandhi (Vowel junction): when two vowels meet. Dirgha Sandhi: a/aa + a/aa = aa (Ram+Ayan = Ramayan). Guna Sandhi: a/aa + i/ii = e (Sur+Indra = Surendra). Vruddhi Sandhi: a/aa + e/ai = ai. Yan Sandhi: i/ii + another vowel = y (Ati+Adhik = Atyadhik). Ayadi Sandhi: e + another = ay (Ne+an = Nayan). (2) Vyanjan Sandhi (Consonant junction): consonant meets vowel or consonant. (3) Visarg Sandhi: Visarg (:) joins with next sound. Important rule: two identical short vowels combine to form one long vowel. Must know: sandhi rules are essential for reading and writing Sanskrit correctly.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Samas (compound words) is the combination of two or more words losing their case endings. Six main types: (1) Avyayibhav: first word is indeclinable (avyay), first word dominant. 'Yathashakti' (according to strength). (2) Tatpurusha: latter word dominant, case relation between parts. 'Rajputrah' (son of king). (3) Karmadharaya: type of Tatpurusha with adjective-noun or comparison. 'Nilkamal' (blue lotus). (4) Dvigu: first word is numeral. 'Trilokah' (collection of three worlds). (5) Dvandva: both words dominant, connected by 'and'. 'Ramalakshmana' (Ram and Lakshman). (6) Bahuvrihi: both words together describe a third person/thing. 'Chakrapanih' (one who has chakra in hand = Vishnu). Method to identify: look at which part is dominant to determine the samas type.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Pratyay (suffixes) are added to verb roots (dhatu) to form different words. Shatru Pratyay (present tense active participant): Pathat (one who is reading), Dhavat (one who is running). Kta Pratyay (past tense adjective): Pathitah (one who has read), Gatah (one who has gone). Tavyat Pratyay (must/should): Pathitavyam (must be read). Dhaturup: conjugation of verb roots in different tenses. Dhat PATH (to read) in Lat Lakar (present tense): Pathati (he reads), Pathataह (they two read), Pathanti (they all read); Pathasi (you read), Pathatah (you two read), Pathatha (you all read); Pathami (I read), Pathavah (we two read), Pathamah (we all read). Lot Lakar (command): Pathatu (let him read). Vidhiling Lakar (should): Pathet (he should read).

subject: Sanskrit
text: Shabdarup: declension of nouns in eight cases (Vibhakti). Ram (masculine a-kaaranta): Prathama: Ramah, Ramau, Ramah. Dwitiya: Ramam, Ramau, Raman. Tritiya: Ramen, Ramabhyam, Ramaih. Chaturthi: Ramaya. Panchami: Ramat. Shashthi: Ramasya. Saptami: Rame. Sambodhan: He Ram! Lata (feminine aa-kaaranta): Lata, Late, Latah. Phalam (neuter a-kaaranta): Phalam, Phale, Phalani. Sarvanaм: Asmad (first person): Aham, Avaam, Vayam. Yusmad (second): Tvam, Yuvam, Yuyam. Tat (third): Sah (masc), Saa (fem), Tat (neuter). Anuvad rules: match case of subject (karta) with appropriate Vibhakti; verb (kriya) must match person (purusha) and number (vachan) of subject. Translation practice is essential for scoring marks.

subject: Sanskrit
text: Vachya (Voice) in Sanskrit: (1) Kartri Vachya (Active Voice): subject is prominent, Parasmaipadi verb used. 'Ramah phalam khadati' (Ram eats fruit). (2) Karma Vachya (Passive Voice): object is prominent, Atmanepadi verb + ya pratyay. 'Ramen phalam khadyate' (Fruit is eaten by Ram). (3) Bhav Vachya (Impersonal Passive): with intransitive verbs, subject becomes agent. 'Ramen hasyate' (Laughing is done by Ram). Rules for conversion: in Karma Vachya the original object takes Prathama Vibhakti; original subject takes Tritiya Vibhakti; verb changes accordingly. Avyay (Indeclinables): words that never change form. Important avyay: adya (today), shvah (tomorrow), hyah (yesterday), atra (here), tatra (there), kutra (where), sada (always), na (not), eva (only/itself), api (also), yadi (if), tada (then), kintu (but), iti (thus/end of quotation).
